# What Exactly Is the Current Model?

The current model does not threshold the factor loadings after fitting an MFA, nor does it retain the "default" and "threshold" modes as two parallel spike-and-slab formulations. It is a **jointly estimated finite mixture of factor analyzers with neuronized sparse loadings**. Its core model is

$$
x_i = \mu_g + \Lambda_g(\alpha_g, W_g, \alpha_0)\eta_i + \varepsilon_{ig}, \qquad z_i = g,
$$

$$
\lambda_{jkg} = T(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)w_{jkg}.
$$

To obtain a genuine point mass at zero, the current spike-and-slab prior explicitly uses

$$
T(t) = t_+ = \max(0, t),
$$

that is, the rectified linear unit (ReLU). Therefore, the final factor-loading element is

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{jkg} = (\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)_+ w_{jkg} = \mathbb{I}(\alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0)(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)w_{jkg}.
}
$$

Here:

- $j = 1, \ldots, p$ indexes observed variables;
- $k = 1, \ldots, q_g$ indexes latent factors in cluster $g$;
- $g = 1, \ldots, G$ indexes mixture components;
- $\alpha_{jkg}$ is a latent activation variable that determines whether the loading crosses the sparsity boundary;
- $\alpha_0$ is a global sparsity threshold shared by all factor loadings;
- $w_{jkg}$ determines the sign and local magnitude of the loading after activation.

Thus, the observation model of the standard MFA remains unchanged. What changes is the prior and parameterization of the factor-loading matrix $\Lambda_g$. Rather than receiving a Gaussian prior directly, $\Lambda_g$ becomes a deterministic function of $(\alpha_g, W_g, \alpha_0)$.

# Before the Modification: Standard Finite MFA

Let

$$
x_i = (x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^p, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, N,
$$

and let $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, G\}$ denote the cluster membership of observation $i$. A standard finite MFA is

$$
z_i \mid \pi \sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_G), \qquad \sum_{g=1}^G \pi_g = 1,
$$

$$
\eta_i \mid z_i = g \sim \mathcal{N}_{q_g}(0, I_{q_g}),
$$

$$
x_i \mid z_i = g, \eta_i, \mu_g, \Lambda_g, \Psi_g \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mu_g + \Lambda_g \eta_i, \Psi_g),
$$

where

$$
\Psi_g = \operatorname{Diag}(\psi_{1g}, \ldots, \psi_{pg}).
$$

After integrating out the factor score $\eta_i$, we obtain

$$
x_i \mid z_i = g \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mu_g, \Sigma_g), \qquad \Sigma_g = \Lambda_g \Lambda_g^\top + \Psi_g,
$$

and the mixture density

$$
f(x_i \mid \Theta) = \sum_{g=1}^G \pi_g \mathcal{N}_p(x_i; \mu_g, \Sigma_g).
$$

In the standard MFA formulation of Murphy, Viroli, and Gormley, a loading row commonly receives the direct prior

$$
\lambda_{jg} = (\lambda_{j1g}, \ldots, \lambda_{j, q_g, g})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_{q_g}(0, I_{q_g}).
$$

This prior is continuous, so loadings may be close to zero but are almost never exactly zero. By itself, it therefore cannot provide explicit posterior inclusion probabilities.

# Point of Entry: Treating Each Factor-Loading Row as a Regression

Let

$$
\mathcal{I}_g = \{i : z_i = g\}, \qquad n_g = |\mathcal{I}_g|,
$$

and stack the factor scores in cluster $g$ as

$$
E_g = \begin{pmatrix} \eta_{i_1}^\top \\ \vdots \\ \eta_{i_{n_g}}^\top \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_g \times q_g}.
$$

For variable $j$, define the centered response

$$
y_{jg} = X_{\mathcal{I}_g, j} - \mu_{jg} \mathbf{1}_{n_g}.
$$

The $j$th observed dimension of the MFA can then be written separately as

$$
y_{jg} = E_g \lambda_{jg} + e_{jg}, \qquad e_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}_{n_g}(0, \psi_{jg} I_{n_g}).
$$

This is exactly a Gaussian regression in which the latent factor scores form the design matrix. Consequently, the neuronized parameterization $\theta_j = T(\alpha_j - \alpha_0)w_j$ of Shin and Liu can be transferred elementwise from regression coefficients to MFA factor loadings: $\theta_j \longrightarrow \lambda_{jkg}$.

Define

$$
a_{jkg} = T(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0),
$$

$$
D_{\alpha, jg} = \operatorname{Diag}(a_{j1g}, \ldots, a_{j, q_g, g}),
$$

$$
w_{jg} = (w_{j1g}, \ldots, w_{j, q_g, g})^\top.
$$

The entire loading row can then be written as

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{jg} = D_{\alpha, jg} w_{jg}.
}
$$

The corresponding row-wise regression becomes

$$
y_{jg} = E_g D_{\alpha, jg} w_{jg} + e_{jg}.
$$

This is the complete structural modification that turns the MFA into a neuronized sparse MFA.

# Why Is This a Spike-and-Slab Prior?

The current specification is

$$
\alpha_{jkg} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad w_{jkg} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_w^2),
$$

with $T(t) = t_+$. It follows that

$$
\gamma_{jkg} := \mathbb{I}(\alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0)
$$

is only a derived quantity determined by $\alpha_{jkg}$ and $\alpha_0$, rather than a Bernoulli latent variable that must be sampled separately.

## Probability of the Spike

When $\alpha_{jkg} \le \alpha_0$, the ReLU output is zero, so

$$
\lambda_{jkg} = 0.
$$

Its prior probability is

$$
P(\lambda_{jkg} = 0 \mid \alpha_0) = P(\alpha_{jkg} \le \alpha_0) = \Phi(\alpha_0).
$$

The corresponding elementwise prior inclusion probability is

$$
\rho_\lambda := P(\lambda_{jkg} \neq 0 \mid \alpha_0) = \Phi(-\alpha_0).
$$

Therefore, to specify an elementwise prior inclusion probability of $\rho_\lambda$, set

$$
\alpha_0 = -\Phi^{-1}(\rho_\lambda) = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \rho_\lambda).
$$

## Form of the Slab

When $\alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0$,

$$
\lambda_{jkg} = (\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)w_{jkg}.
$$

The marginal prior can therefore be written as

$$
p(\lambda_{jkg} \mid \alpha_0) = \Phi(\alpha_0)\delta_0(\lambda_{jkg}) + \Phi(-\alpha_0) p_{\mathrm{slab}}(\lambda_{jkg} \mid \alpha_0, \tau_w),
$$

where $\delta_0$ is a point mass at zero and the continuous slab is the product of the truncated Gaussian variable $(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)$ and the Gaussian weight $w_{jkg}$. More explicitly,

$$
p_{\mathrm{slab}}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{\Phi(-\alpha_0)} \int_{\alpha_0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\tau_w(a - \alpha_0)} \phi\!\left( \frac{\lambda}{\tau_w(a - \alpha_0)} \right) \phi(a) \, da.
$$

This is not an additional Gaussian slab imposed by hand. It is the continuous slab induced automatically by the neuronized parameterization. ReLU produces a discrete spike-and-slab prior with Laplace-like tails.

## Distinct Roles of $\alpha_0$ and $\tau_w$

Because $E(w_{jkg}) = 0$,

$$
E(\lambda_{jkg} \mid \alpha_0) = 0.
$$

Moreover,

$$
E(\lambda_{jkg}^2 \mid \alpha_0) = \tau_w^2 E\{(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)_+^2\},
$$

and for standard-normal $\alpha_{jkg}$,

$$
E\{(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)_+^2\} = (1 + \alpha_0^2)\Phi(-\alpha_0) - \alpha_0 \phi(\alpha_0).
$$

Therefore:

- $\alpha_0$ primarily controls how many factor loadings are activated, but it also changes their post-activation scale;
- $\tau_w$ primarily controls the overall magnitude of nonzero factor loadings;
- the two cannot be interpreted as completely independent "selection" and "effect-size" parameters.

# Complete Hierarchical Model

The current finite neuronized sparse MFA can be written as

$$
\pi \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_G),
$$

$$
z_i \mid \pi \sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\pi),
$$

$$
\eta_i \mid z_i = g \sim \mathcal{N}_{q_g}(0, I_{q_g}),
$$

$$
x_i \mid z_i = g, \eta_i, \mu_g, \Lambda_g, \Psi_g \sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mu_g + \Lambda_g \eta_i, \Psi_g),
$$

$$
\Psi_g = \operatorname{Diag}(\psi_{1g}, \ldots, \psi_{pg}),
$$

$$
\mu_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_{0j}, s_{\mu j}^2), \qquad \psi_{jg} \sim \operatorname{IG}(a_\psi, b_{\psi j}),
$$

$$
\alpha_{jkg} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad w_{jkg} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_w^2),
$$

$$
\lambda_{jkg} = (\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)_+ w_{jkg}.
$$

To learn the overall degree of sparsity from the data, one may specify

$$
\rho_\lambda = \Phi(-\alpha_0), \qquad \rho_\lambda \sim \operatorname{Beta}(a_0, b_0).
$$

By change of variables, the induced prior for $\alpha_0$ is

$$
p(\alpha_0) \propto \Phi(-\alpha_0)^{a_0 - 1} \{1 - \Phi(-\alpha_0)\}^{b_0 - 1} \phi(\alpha_0).
$$

The main model contains only this single neuronized spike-and-slab formulation. One global $\alpha_0$ controls the overall sparsity of all loading elements across all clusters.

# How Do Sparse Factor Loadings Change the Within-Cluster Covariance?

For cluster $g$, the marginal covariance remains

$$
\Sigma_g = \Lambda_g \Lambda_g^\top + \Psi_g.
$$

However, its $(j, \ell)$th element is now

$$
(\Sigma_g)_{j\ell} = \sum_{k=1}^{q_g} T(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0) T(\alpha_{\ell kg} - \alpha_0) w_{jkg} w_{\ell kg} + \mathbb{I}(j = \ell)\psi_{jg}.
$$

Thus, the neuronized prior directly determines which variables can generate covariance through shared factors.

If the entire loading row of variable $j$ in cluster $g$ is zero, so that $\lambda_{jg} = 0$, then

$$
(\Sigma_g)_{j\ell} = 0, \qquad \ell \neq j,
$$

and

$$
(\Sigma_g)_{jj} = \psi_{jg}.
$$

Variable $j$ still retains its own mean and independent noise, but no longer participates in the low-rank shared covariance of that cluster. Accordingly, variable selection here means **variable selection within the shared within-cluster covariance structure**; it does not remove the original data column from the entire likelihood.

# From Elementwise Spikes to Loading-Row Selection

Define the elementwise activity indicator

$$
\gamma_{jkg} = \mathbb{I}(\alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0).
$$

The row-level event that variable $j$ enters at least one factor in cluster $g$ is

$$
r_{jg} = \mathbb{I}\!\left( \max_{1 \le k \le q_g} \alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0 \right) = \mathbb{I}\!\left( \sum_{k=1}^{q_g} \gamma_{jkg} > 0 \right).
$$

The elementwise and row-level posterior inclusion probabilities are therefore

$$
\operatorname{PIP}_{jkg} = P(\alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0 \mid X),
$$

$$
\operatorname{rowPIP}_{jg} = P\!\left( \max_k \alpha_{jkg} > \alpha_0 \mid X \right).
$$

If $M$ MCMC draws are retained, then

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{PIP}}_{jkg} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \mathbb{I}\!\left( \alpha_{jkg}^{(m)} > \alpha_0^{(m)} \right),
$$

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{rowPIP}}_{jg} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \mathbb{I}\!\left( \max_k \alpha_{jkg}^{(m)} > \alpha_0^{(m)} \right).
$$

`rowPIP >= 0.5` provides a transparent median-probability decision rule. If control of selection errors is required, Bayesian false discovery rate (FDR) can instead be controlled using the ordered values of $1 - \operatorname{rowPIP}$.

The row event is more appropriate as the primary variable-selection target than inclusion in a particular factor. Sign changes or permutations of factor columns do not alter a row-level PIP. More generally, for any invertible orthogonal rotation $R$,

$$
\lambda_{jg} = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \lambda_{jg}^\top R = 0.
$$

Thus, whether an entire row is zero is rotation invariant. In contrast, the elementwise PIP for a particular $k$ depends on the factor orientation selected by the sparse prior and should be interpreted as a secondary result.

## Prior Row-Inclusion Probability for Different $q_g$

Conditional on the global $\alpha_0$, with independent $\alpha_{jkg}$,

$$
P(r_{jg} = 0 \mid \alpha_0) = \Phi(\alpha_0)^{q_g},
$$

so

$$
\boxed{
P(r_{jg} = 1 \mid \alpha_0) = 1 - \Phi(\alpha_0)^{q_g}.
}
$$

This means that a global $\alpha_0$ equalizes the **elementwise inclusion probability**, not the row-level inclusion probability. As $q_g$ increases, the prior probability that at least one loading in a row is active also increases. This is the explicit mathematical implication of the current unified model and should not be described as giving all clusters the same row sparsity.

# Joint Posterior

Define the residual

$$
r_{ijg} = x_{ij} - \mu_{jg} - \sum_{k=1}^{q_g} T(\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)w_{jkg}\eta_{ik}.
$$

Ignoring constants that do not depend on the parameters, the complete-data posterior kernel is

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\pi, z, \eta, \mu, \Psi, \alpha, W, \alpha_0 \mid X) &\propto \prod_{i=1}^N \prod_{g=1}^G \left[ \pi_g \phi_{q_g}(\eta_i; 0, I_{q_g}) \prod_{j=1}^p \psi_{jg}^{-1/2} \exp\!\left( -\frac{r_{ijg}^2}{2\psi_{jg}} \right) \right]^{\mathbb{I}(z_i = g)} \\
&\quad \times p(\pi) \prod_{g=1}^G \prod_{j=1}^p p(\mu_{jg}) p(\psi_{jg}) \prod_{g=1}^G \prod_{j=1}^p \prod_{k=1}^{q_g} \phi(\alpha_{jkg}) \phi(w_{jkg}; 0, \tau_w^2) p(\alpha_0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Its log-kernel can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log p(\cdot \mid X) &= \sum_{i=1}^N \log \pi_{z_i} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_g} \sum_{j=1}^p \left[ \log \psi_{jg} + \frac{r_{ijg}^2}{\psi_{jg}} \right] \\
&\quad - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N \eta_i^\top \eta_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{g, j, k} \alpha_{jkg}^2 - \frac{1}{2\tau_w^2} \sum_{g, j, k} w_{jkg}^2 \\
&\quad + \log p(\pi) + \log p(\mu) + \log p(\Psi) + \log p(\alpha_0) + C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Relative to the standard MFA, the new nonlinearity appears only in $r_{ijg} = r_{ijg}(\alpha, W, \alpha_0)$. The remaining mixture and factor-analysis structures are unchanged.

# MCMC Full Conditionals and Update Scheme

## Updating the Mixing Weights $\pi$

If

$$
\pi \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_G),
$$

and

$$
n_g = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(z_i = g),
$$

then

$$
\boxed{
\pi \mid z \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(\delta_1 + n_1, \ldots, \delta_G + n_G).
}
$$

## Updating the Factor Scores $\eta_i$

For $z_i = g$, define

$$
V_{\eta, g} = \left( I_{q_g} + \Lambda_g^\top \Psi_g^{-1} \Lambda_g \right)^{-1},
$$

$$
m_{\eta, ig} = V_{\eta, g} \Lambda_g^\top \Psi_g^{-1} (x_i - \mu_g).
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\eta_i \mid - \sim \mathcal{N}_{q_g}(m_{\eta, ig}, V_{\eta, g}).
}
$$

This full conditional is identical to that of the standard MFA; it only uses the current $\Lambda_g$ reconstructed from $(\alpha, W, \alpha_0)$.

## Updating the Neuronized Factor-Loading Block

For each $(j, g)$, write again

$$
y_{jg} = H_{jg} w_{jg} + e_{jg},
$$

where

$$
H_{jg} = E_g D_{\alpha, jg}, \qquad e_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jg} I).
$$

### Step One: Integrate Out $w_{jg}$ and Update $\alpha_{jg}$

From

$$
w_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_w^2 I_{q_g}),
$$

we obtain the collapsed model

$$
y_{jg} \mid \alpha_{jg}, E_g, \psi_{jg}, \alpha_0 \sim \mathcal{N}_{n_g}(0, \Omega_{jg}),
$$

$$
\Omega_{jg} = \psi_{jg} I_{n_g} + \tau_w^2 H_{jg} H_{jg}^\top.
$$

Therefore, the collapsed log-likelihood for $\alpha_{jg}$ is

$$
\ell_{jg}(\alpha_{jg}) = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \log|\Omega_{jg}| + y_{jg}^\top \Omega_{jg}^{-1} y_{jg} \right].
$$

Because $\alpha_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_{q_g})$, elliptical slice sampling (ESS) can be used directly. Draw

$$
\nu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_{q_g}),
$$

and propose along the ellipse

$$
\alpha_{jg}(\varphi) = \alpha_{jg}^{\mathrm{old}} \cos \varphi + \nu \sin \varphi.
$$

ESS repeatedly shrinks the search interval for $\varphi$ until

$$
\ell_{jg}\{\alpha_{jg}(\varphi)\} > \ell_{jg}(\alpha_{jg}^{\mathrm{old}}) + \log u, \qquad u \sim \operatorname{Unif}(0, 1).
$$

This step requires neither a Bernoulli full conditional for $\gamma_{jkg}$ nor tuning of a random-walk proposal scale.

Computationally, there is no need to construct the $n_g \times n_g$ matrix $\Omega_{jg}$. Define

$$
B_{jg} = I_{q_g} + \frac{\tau_w^2}{\psi_{jg}} H_{jg}^\top H_{jg},
$$

The matrix determinant lemma gives

$$
\log|\Omega_{jg}| = n_g \log \psi_{jg} + \log|B_{jg}|,
$$

and the Woodbury identity gives

$$
y_{jg}^\top \Omega_{jg}^{-1} y_{jg} = \frac{y_{jg}^\top y_{jg}}{\psi_{jg}} - \frac{\tau_w^2}{\psi_{jg}^2} y_{jg}^\top H_{jg} B_{jg}^{-1} H_{jg}^\top y_{jg}.
$$

Thus, each ESS likelihood evaluation requires operations only on a $q_g \times q_g$ matrix.

### Step Two: Update $w_{jg}$ Given the New $\alpha_{jg}$

Define

$$
K_{w, jg} = \tau_w^{-2} I_{q_g} + \psi_{jg}^{-1} H_{jg}^\top H_{jg},
$$

$$
V_{w, jg} = K_{w, jg}^{-1},
$$

$$
m_{w, jg} = V_{w, jg} \psi_{jg}^{-1} H_{jg}^\top y_{jg}.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
w_{jg} \mid - \sim \mathcal{N}_{q_g}(m_{w, jg}, V_{w, jg}).
}
$$

Finally, reconstruct

$$
\boxed{
\lambda_{jg} = D_{\alpha, jg} w_{jg}.
}
$$

Algorithm 1 of Shin and Liu uses coordinatewise random-walk Metropolis--Hastings (RWMH) for the same collapsed target and then samples $w$ from its conditional Gaussian distribution. Replacing RWMH with ESS in the current project is a computational implementation choice. It changes neither the neuronized prior nor the target posterior and directly exploits the standard Gaussian prior on $\alpha$.

## Learning the Global Threshold $\alpha_0$

If $\alpha_0$ is fixed, this step is skipped. If

$$
\Phi(-\alpha_0) \sim \operatorname{Beta}(a_0, b_0),
$$

then a simple random-walk update for $\alpha_0$ conditional on all $\alpha_{jkg}$ should be avoided because $\alpha_0$ is strongly correlated with all activation variables.

Let

$$
M_\alpha = p \sum_{g=1}^G q_g
$$

be the total number of activation variables. Use the group move of Shin and Liu:

$$
(\alpha, \alpha_0) \longrightarrow (\alpha + \delta \mathbf{1}, \alpha_0 + \delta).
$$

Because

$$
(\alpha_{jkg} + \delta) - (\alpha_0 + \delta) = \alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0,
$$

this move leaves every activation state, factor loading, and likelihood contribution unchanged. It moves only along the strongly correlated translation direction of the posterior.

When $a_0 = b_0 = 1$, $p(\alpha_0) \propto \phi(\alpha_0)$, and

$$
\boxed{
\delta \mid - \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left( -\frac{\sum_{g, j, k} \alpha_{jkg} + \alpha_0}{M_\alpha + 1}, \frac{1}{M_\alpha + 1} \right).
}
$$

When $(a_0, b_0) \neq (1, 1)$, the one-dimensional log-target for $\delta$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log g(\delta) &= -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{g, j, k}(\alpha_{jkg} + \delta)^2 - \frac{1}{2}(\alpha_0 + \delta)^2 \\
&\quad + (a_0 - 1) \log \Phi\{-(\alpha_0 + \delta)\} + (b_0 - 1) \log \left[1 - \Phi\{-(\alpha_0 + \delta)\}\right] + C,
\end{aligned}
$$

which can be sampled by one-dimensional slice sampling or by the multiple-try Metropolized independence sampler proposed in the original paper. After the group move, $\alpha_{jg}$ must still be updated row by row because the group move itself does not change any inclusion state.

## Updating the Cluster Means $\mu_{jg}$

Define

$$
u_{ijg} = x_{ij} - \lambda_{jg}^\top \eta_i.
$$

If

$$
\mu_{jg} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_{0j}, s_{\mu j}^2),
$$

then

$$
V_{\mu, jg} = \left( s_{\mu j}^{-2} + n_g \psi_{jg}^{-1} \right)^{-1},
$$

$$
m_{\mu, jg} = V_{\mu, jg} \left( s_{\mu j}^{-2} m_{0j} + \psi_{jg}^{-1} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_g} u_{ijg} \right),
$$

$$
\boxed{
\mu_{jg} \mid - \sim \mathcal{N}(m_{\mu, jg}, V_{\mu, jg}).
}
$$

## Updating the Uniqueness Variances $\psi_{jg}$

If

$$
\psi_{jg} \sim \operatorname{IG}(a_\psi, b_{\psi j}),
$$

then

$$
\boxed{
\psi_{jg} \mid - \sim \operatorname{IG}\!\left( a_\psi + \frac{n_g}{2}, b_{\psi j} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_g} r_{ijg}^2 \right).
}
$$

## Updating the Allocations $z_i$

When updating cluster allocations, integrate out the factor scores:

$$
P(z_i = g \mid -) \propto \pi_g \mathcal{N}_p(x_i; \mu_g, \Sigma_g),
$$

$$
\Sigma_g = \Lambda_g \Lambda_g^\top + \Psi_g.
$$

To avoid directly inverting a $p \times p$ matrix, define

$$
C_g = I_{q_g} + \Lambda_g^\top \Psi_g^{-1} \Lambda_g.
$$

Then

$$
\log|\Sigma_g| = \log|\Psi_g| + \log|C_g|,
$$

$$
\Sigma_g^{-1} = \Psi_g^{-1} - \Psi_g^{-1} \Lambda_g C_g^{-1} \Lambda_g^\top \Psi_g^{-1}.
$$

Thus, cluster allocations can still be updated using only $q_g \times q_g$ linear algebra.

# One Complete MCMC Iteration

Each iteration proceeds in the following order:

1. Update the mixing proportions $\pi$ from the current $z$.
2. Update the factor score $\eta_i$ of each observation using the current neuronized $\Lambda_g$.
3. For each cluster $g$ and variable $j$:
   - integrate out $w_{jg}$ and update $\alpha_{jg}$ using ESS;
   - given the new $\alpha_{jg}$, update $w_{jg}$ from its Gaussian full conditional;
   - compute $\lambda_{jg} = D_{\alpha, jg} w_{jg}$.
4. If $\alpha_0$ is learned, update $(\alpha, \alpha_0)$ using the common-shift group move.
5. Update $\mu_g$ and $\Psi_g$.
6. Update the cluster allocations $z_i$ using the marginal covariance $\Sigma_g = \Lambda_g \Lambda_g^\top + \Psi_g$.
7. Save $z$, $\Lambda$, $\alpha$, $\alpha_0$, $W$, $\Psi$, and the derived inclusion states.
8. After warm-up, use the retained draws to compute row-level PIPs, elementwise PIPs, posterior covariance means, and the posterior similarity matrix.

`allocation_start` only delays Step 6 in the implementation so that the factor loadings can first learn a stable structure from the initial partition. It is not part of the model.


# Final Interpretation

After introducing the neuronized spike-and-slab prior, our MFA can be summarized as follows:

> Each cluster is still represented by a factor analyzer, but each factor loading is no longer drawn directly from a Gaussian prior. Instead, it is generated by multiplying a Gaussian weight by the amount by which a Gaussian activation variable exceeds a global threshold. A loading whose activation variable does not exceed the threshold is exactly zero; an activated loading contributes to the low-rank covariance. Clustering and variable selection therefore share the same sparse covariance parameters and are learned jointly within one MCMC chain.

The most compact complete specification is

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
z_i &\sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\pi),\\
\eta_i \mid z_i = g &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_{q_g}),\\
x_i \mid z_i = g, \eta_i &\sim \mathcal{N}_p(\mu_g + \Lambda_g \eta_i, \Psi_g),\\
\lambda_{jkg} &= (\alpha_{jkg} - \alpha_0)_+ w_{jkg},\\
\alpha_{jkg} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1),\\
w_{jkg} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_w^2),\\
\Phi(-\alpha_0) &\sim \operatorname{Beta}(a_0, b_0).
\end{aligned}
}
$$
